source.title: Mentoring posts and talks for young African entrepreneurs
source.attribution: A summary of Strive Masiyiwa's mentoring posts on Facebook and his public talks and interviews. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the posts, which are in copyright. The posts sit behind a Facebook login, so themes were confirmed via news coverage of them (The Standard, Kenya; News Ghana; AP) and via his own talks and interviews (Stanford GSB, Forbes Africa, McKinsey, How We Made It in Africa).

cards.title: Learn the rules and language of your field
cards.body:
Masiyiwa tells young entrepreneurs that every industry has its own rules, terms and ways of doing things. If you don't understand them, established players won't take you seriously and doors stay closed.

Taking time to master that language, through reading, courses, mentors and listening carefully, gives you credibility and access to the networks where deals happen. It's an investment that pays off whichever sector you enter.
cards.apply_it: List five terms or rules in your field you only half-understand, and learn one properly this week.

quiz.question: Why does Masiyiwa stress learning an industry's rules and language?
options: It earns credibility and access to established networks
So you can ignore them later
quiz.explanation: Understanding how a field works lets newcomers be taken seriously and gain access.

cards.title: Be willing to say no to bribes, even at a cost
cards.body:
In widely shared posts, Masiyiwa wrote that he has never paid a bribe and has turned down demands from powerful people, sometimes losing contracts as a result. He argued that corruption is not only a government problem; it is common in business too, and fighting it is everyone's responsibility.

For anyone building a career or company, deciding your line in advance makes it easier to hold under pressure. A reputation for integrity takes years to build and can be lost in one deal.
cards.apply_it: Write down one ethical line you won't cross at work, and what you'd say if someone asked you to cross it.

quiz.question: What point did Masiyiwa make about corruption?
options: It also happens in business, and everyone must resist it
quiz.explanation: He said some of the worst corruption he saw was in the private sector and urged personal responsibility.

cards.title: Don't confuse a flashy lifestyle with business success
cards.body:
Masiyiwa has warned young people against measuring success by luxury cars, designer watches and holidays shown online. Display isn't the same as a business that lasts.

He noted that many genuinely wealthy people he met lived simply, with their wealth showing in their investments rather than their clothes. Focusing on building something solid, and meeting responsibilities like children's education first, matters more than looking successful.
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing you spend on mainly to look successful, and redirect that money to your business or savings for a month.

quiz.question: According to Masiyiwa, where did the wealth of many rich people he met show up?
quiz.explanation: He observed that real wealth often sits quietly in investments, not in visible luxuries.

cards.title: Keep investing in your own skills
cards.body:
A theme of the lessons Masiyiwa shares from his own career is to set aside time and money to improve yourself, through training, reading and learning new skills, even when you're passed over or nobody is paying for it.

He also encourages young people to value practical, skilled trades and skills-based businesses rather than only buying and reselling goods. Skills are an asset no one can take from you, and they open opportunities that trading alone can't.
cards.apply_it: Budget a small amount of time and money each month for one course, book or skill that would make you more valuable.

quiz.question: What does Masiyiwa advise doing even when you're overlooked for opportunities?
options: Wait for someone to notice you
Keep investing your own time and money in your skills
quiz.explanation: He urges ongoing self-investment, since skills create opportunities regardless of setbacks.

cards.title: Look for the opportunity inside the problem
cards.body:
A theme Masiyiwa returns to is that problems are where business opportunities hide. He has said that needs are the playground of entrepreneurs, and he has used his Facebook page to discuss gaps such as sanitation, where many people still lack running water and toilets, as openings for new businesses.

His own company grew from the fact that most Africans had no phone access in the early 1990s. Rather than complaining about what's missing, ask who would pay for a solution.
cards.apply_it: Write down three things that frustrate people in your community. For each, ask: who would pay to have this solved?

quiz.question: How does Masiyiwa view problems like poor sanitation?
options: As problems too big to touch
quiz.explanation: He frames unmet needs as the playground of entrepreneurs.

cards.title: Save, and live within your means
cards.body:
In a Facebook post Masiyiwa credited his mother's frugality, describing a household where saving and living within one's means were taken very seriously, with small sums put aside for hard times. He observed that people who fail in business often lack discipline in saving.

Saving isn't only about having a cushion; it trains the self-control that running a business demands. Spending less than you earn, even by a small margin, gives you room to survive setbacks and seize opportunities.
cards.apply_it: Set up a small automatic saving, even a modest amount, on the day you get paid this month.

quiz.question: What did Masiyiwa observe about people who fail in business?
options: They often lack discipline in saving
quiz.explanation: He links business failure to weak saving discipline.

cards.title: Master three basics: reading, counting and selling
cards.body:
Masiyiwa has described reading, counting and selling as the core skills of business, and says he started building them as a child, when his mother had him sell chewing gum at school. Reading has been a constant theme on his Facebook page, where he says he urged followers from the start to read widely.

These basics compound. Reading widens what you know, numeracy keeps you honest about profit and loss, and selling turns ideas into income. Weakness in any one of them can sink an otherwise good business.
cards.apply_it: Rate yourself from 1 to 5 on reading, counting and selling. Pick the weakest and do one thing to improve it this week.

quiz.question: Which three skills does Masiyiwa call the basics of business?
options: Networking, dressing well and public speaking
quiz.explanation: He traces his business foundation to reading, numeracy and selling.

cards.title: Try the product yourself before you rely on it
cards.body:
Masiyiwa has written that, as an entrepreneur, he never wants to depend on a product without having tried something like it himself, and he urged followers to take the same approach in their own fields.

Using a product or service as a customer would shows you its strengths, frustrations and gaps far better than a report can. Whether you're choosing a supplier, launching your own offering or studying a competitor, first-hand experience is the quickest route to understanding.
cards.apply_it: This week, use your own product or service, or a competitor's, exactly as a customer would, and note three things that annoy you.

quiz.question: What practice does Masiyiwa recommend about products in your field?
options: Try them yourself before relying on them
quiz.explanation: First-hand use reveals what reports miss.

cards.title: Look at the business side of everything
cards.body:
Masiyiwa encourages young people to develop a business mind by asking how things around them make money. He has described quizzing a ride-hailing driver about how the app worked, and noted that most football fans study the game rather than how their club is run as a business.

This habit of commercial curiosity trains you to spot models you could adapt, for example to local transport problems. Every shop, app and service is a free case study if you ask how it earns and what it costs.
cards.apply_it: Pick one business you use daily and work out how it makes money and what its biggest costs might be.

quiz.question: What habit does Masiyiwa encourage with everyday services like ride-hailing apps?
options: Asking how they make money and work as businesses
Only using them as a customer
quiz.explanation: He wants young people to study the commercial side of what they see.

cards.title: Customers should never have to beg to do business with you
cards.body:
Masiyiwa recalls dealing with a struggling phone maker whose executives treated his team with arrogance. He took it as a sign the company was in trouble and prepared his business to switch to other platforms, a call that proved right.

His lesson: attitude determines how far you go. A business where customers or partners feel they must beg for attention has a serious problem, however successful it looks today. Humility and responsiveness keep people coming back.
cards.apply_it: Ask two recent customers or colleagues how easy you are to deal with, and act on one thing they say.

quiz.question: What did Masiyiwa take as a warning sign in the phone maker's executives?
quiz.explanation: He reads arrogance towards customers as a sign of decline.

cards.title: Be ready for a long fight when the cause is right
cards.body:
Masiyiwa's best-known story, which he shared in installments on Facebook, is his years-long legal battle for a licence to run a mobile network in Zimbabwe. He lost contracts, faced financial pressure and could have given up, but kept going until the courts ruled the state monopoly unconstitutional and Econet could launch.

Not every battle is worth that cost, but when you're confident you're right, persistence through legitimate means can change the rules for everyone who comes after you.
cards.apply_it: Name one goal you dropped when it got hard. Is it worth another, better-planned attempt?

quiz.question: How did Masiyiwa win the right to launch his mobile network?
options: By giving up and moving abroad
Through a years-long court battle he refused to abandon
quiz.explanation: Persistence through the courts eventually ended the monopoly.

cards.title: Prepare and rehearse before a big pitch
cards.body:
Masiyiwa has told how a small team he backed bid for a mobile licence in Botswana against far larger, established companies. They spent weeks planning and running mock presentations, and came out on top.

Preparation is one of the few advantages a small player can fully control. Rehearsing your pitch, anticipating hard questions and knowing your numbers cold can outweigh the brand and budget of a bigger rival.
cards.apply_it: Before your next important meeting, rehearse it out loud with someone who will ask you tough questions.

quiz.question: How did Masiyiwa's small team beat larger rivals for the Botswana licence?
options: Through weeks of planning and mock pitches
quiz.explanation: Thorough preparation helped them outperform bigger firms.

cards.title: Be clear about why you're investing
cards.body:
In a Facebook series for Africans living abroad who want to invest back home, Masiyiwa's first step was to know your motive. Is it to reduce the money you send home, to create a path to return, to build a retirement nest egg or to earn a better return?

Your motive should shape your strategy. Without it, it's easy to be drawn into investments that sound exciting but don't serve what you actually want.
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence explaining why you want to invest. Check whether your current or planned investments match it.

quiz.question: What did Masiyiwa say diaspora investors should be clear about first?
quiz.explanation: Knowing your motive keeps your investments aligned with your goals.

cards.title: Be honest about how much time you can give a business
cards.body:
Another step in Masiyiwa's advice to diaspora investors is an honest look at your time. With a full-time job, distance and time-zone differences, how much attention can you really give a business back home?

He urged people to decide what success looks like, what can be delegated, who their local contact is and how experienced they are, and to do thorough due diligence. A business that needs more time than you have is likely to struggle.
cards.apply_it: Estimate the hours per week your business idea needs, then compare it with the hours you can realistically give.

quiz.question: What did Masiyiwa urge diaspora investors to assess honestly?
options: How famous the business can get
How much time they can give the business
How quickly they can sell it
quiz.explanation: Available time should shape the type of business and its timing.

cards.title: Ask many people, and ask the same question more than once
cards.body:
Masiyiwa advises people starting a business to seek advice from those who have done it, with detailed, well-researched questions. His technique: ask different questions of the same person, and the same question of different people, then draw your own conclusions.

This guards against relying on one person's bias or a single success story. Decisions based on rumour or a whim, he warns, are a serious mistake.
cards.apply_it: Pick a decision you're facing. Ask three experienced people the same key question and compare their answers.

quiz.question: What advice-gathering technique does Masiyiwa recommend?
options: Trust the first person you ask
Ask the same question of different people and different questions of the same person
quiz.explanation: Triangulating advice helps you reach your own informed view.

cards.title: Choose managers for competence, not loyalty
cards.body:
Masiyiwa warns that trusting a relative is not enough reason to hand them your money or your business. When choosing who will run things day to day, he urges people to pick on competence, be professional even if the person is family, and set clear accountability with agreed deliverables.

Many family businesses fail because roles are given out of obligation rather than skill. Clear expectations protect both the business and the relationship.
cards.apply_it: If someone close to you handles your money or business, write down what you expect from them and agree it together.

quiz.question: What does Masiyiwa say about putting relatives in charge of a business?
options: Choose on competence and set clear accountability, even with family
Always choose family because they're loyal
Let them decide their own duties
quiz.explanation: Competence and accountability matter more than family ties.

cards.title: Approach business with humility; nothing is simple
cards.body:
Masiyiwa has cautioned against arrogance in business, writing that it requires humility and respect, and that nothing is truly simple. People who assume they already know everything rarely ask the questions that would save them.

Humility here isn't weakness. It means respecting the complexity of a market, listening to people with experience and accepting that you'll need to keep learning. It's often the newcomer who thinks a business is easy who loses the most.
cards.apply_it: Think of a project you've assumed would be easy. Write down three things that could go wrong and how you'd handle them.

quiz.question: What attitude does Masiyiwa say business requires?
quiz.explanation: He warns that nothing in business is truly simple.

cards.title: Offer a share of the business to attract good people
cards.body:
Masiyiwa notes that small and new businesses often struggle to attract talented staff, because joining them is risky. His suggestion is to consider offering shares, so people are rewarded for the risk they take. He has described equity as the currency that makes strong hires affordable.

Ownership also changes behaviour: people who own part of a business tend to care more about its long-term success. Done carefully, with clear terms, sharing equity can help a young company punch above its weight.
cards.apply_it: If you run a small venture, think about one key person you'd love to hire. Could a share of future success be part of the offer?

quiz.question: What does Masiyiwa suggest small businesses offer to attract talent?
options: A share of ownership in the business
quiz.explanation: Equity compensates people for the risk of joining a young firm.

cards.title: Hire for passion and contribution, not just paperwork
cards.body:
When building a team, Masiyiwa advises looking past certificates to what a person can actually contribute, and hiring people who are passionate about the product. He has said loyalty alone isn't the goal.

Credentials show what someone has studied; passion and capability show what they'll do. A small team of people who care deeply about the work can outperform a larger group that's just collecting a salary.
cards.apply_it: In your next hire or team choice, ask each candidate to show something they've built or done, not just their qualifications.

quiz.question: What does Masiyiwa look for beyond credentials when hiring?
options: Passion for the product and what the person can contribute
quiz.explanation: He prioritises passion and real contribution.

cards.title: Keep improving your product, or someone else will
cards.body:
Masiyiwa calls innovation the new form of capital. He has said that if your first product doesn't embarrass you within a year, you aren't innovating fast enough. Turning an idea into a product is only the start; the work continues in constantly improving it.

Technology can make yesterday's methods obsolete quickly. Businesses that keep asking how to serve customers better stay ahead, while those that stand still are overtaken.
cards.apply_it: Look at your main product or service and list one improvement you could test in the next month.

quiz.question: How does Masiyiwa describe innovation?
options: As the new form of capital
As a luxury for big companies
quiz.explanation: He sees continuous innovation as a key asset.

cards.title: Build trust through relationships, not just transactions
cards.body:
Masiyiwa argues that trust comes from genuine relationships rather than one-off deals. When he launched mobile money in a country where people had lost faith in banks, his team won people over by engaging them directly and openly rather than relying only on advertising.

In any field, people do business with those they trust. Showing up, keeping your word and caring about the other person's interests builds a reputation no marketing budget can buy.
cards.apply_it: Contact one customer, supplier or colleague this week with no request attached, just to ask how they're doing.

quiz.question: Where does Masiyiwa say trust comes from?
options: Genuine relationships rather than one-off transactions
quiz.explanation: He describes trust as built through non-transactional relationships.

cards.title: Get people talking about your product
cards.body:
To launch mobile money, Masiyiwa's team hired university students to start conversations about it on city buses, aiming to spread word of mouth until it reached a tipping point. He said there was no other marketing.

Recommendations from ordinary people often persuade more than advertising does, especially for something new that people are wary of. Making your product easy and worth talking about, then helping people share it, can be cheaper and more powerful than paid promotion.
cards.apply_it: Ask your three happiest customers if they'd tell one friend about you, and make it easy for them to do so.

quiz.question: How did Masiyiwa's team market mobile money at launch?
options: By spreading word of mouth through conversations on buses
quiz.explanation: They relied on conversations to build awareness and trust.

cards.title: Start giving early, not after you're rich
cards.body:
Masiyiwa advises entrepreneurs to build giving into their plans from the start, suggesting they register a foundation alongside their company rather than waiting until they've made their fortune. He and his wife founded Higherlife Foundation, which supports orphaned and disadvantaged children through education.

The principle scales down to anyone. Generosity is a habit; if you wait until you feel wealthy enough, you may never start. Giving a little now shapes who you become.
cards.apply_it: Choose a cause you care about and commit a small, regular amount of money or time to it starting this month.

quiz.question: When does Masiyiwa suggest entrepreneurs start giving?
options: From the start, alongside building the company
quiz.explanation: He recommends building philanthropy in from day one.

cards.title: Keep a clear line between business and politics
cards.body:
Masiyiwa has said he sought a clear boundary between business and politics, and did not let political connections drive how he ran his companies. His own experience, fighting a state monopoly in court, showed how dangerous it can be when business depends on political favour.

Businesses built on connections can collapse when the connections change. Competing on the quality of your product and service is slower, but it gives you independence and a reputation that survives changes in power.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: if a key contact lost their position tomorrow, would your work survive? If not, what would make it more independent?

quiz.question: What boundary does Masiyiwa emphasise?
options: A clear separation between business and politics
quiz.explanation: He avoided letting political connections drive his business.

cards.title: Recognise and back women entrepreneurs
cards.body:
Masiyiwa has called African women entrepreneurs the heartbeat of entrepreneurship on the continent, and regularly highlights women-led businesses on his Facebook page. He has spoken against laws and traditions that stop women owning land or building wealth, even though they grow much of Africa's food.

Backing women in business, as customers, partners, investors or family members, widens the talent pool and strengthens households. Removing barriers for half the population is one of the fastest routes to shared prosperity.
cards.apply_it: Make a point of buying from, recommending or mentoring one woman-led business this month.

quiz.question: How has Masiyiwa described African women entrepreneurs?
options: As a minor part of the economy
As the heartbeat of entrepreneurship in Africa
quiz.explanation: He highlights their central role and the barriers they face.

cards.title: Show commitment with your own stake
cards.body:
Masiyiwa has told how he started his first business with very little money and went to a bank for a loan. The banker asked if he owned the car outside and suggested he sell it, promising to match the amount as proof of his commitment. He sold the car, returned with the cash and got his backing.

Lenders and partners want to see that you're willing to risk something yourself. Putting in your own savings, time or assets, however modest, signals that you believe in what you're building.
cards.apply_it: If you're seeking support for an idea, decide what you'll personally put in first, and say so when you ask.

quiz.question: What did the banker ask Masiyiwa to do to prove his commitment?
options: Sell his car and bring in the money
quiz.explanation: Putting in his own stake convinced the bank to back him.

cards.title: Don't accept second-rate standards for African markets
cards.body:
Masiyiwa rejects the idea that products and services for Africa should be scaled-down versions of those elsewhere. He argues the continent is part of the global technology landscape and should expect the same standards, pointing to how mobile money in Africa leapfrogged traditional banking.

For entrepreneurs, this is a call to aim for world-class quality rather than settling because 'it's good enough here'. Customers everywhere deserve excellent products, and building to that bar makes your business competitive anywhere.
cards.apply_it: Compare your product or service with the best version in the world. Name one gap you could close.

quiz.question: What is Masiyiwa's view on standards for African markets?
options: Lower standards are fine for Africa
Only imported products should be used
Quality doesn't matter if prices are low
Africa should expect the same world-class standards as elsewhere
quiz.explanation: He rejects scaling back products or standards for African markets.

cards.title: Build brands around local produce
cards.body:
Masiyiwa sees agriculture as one of Africa's biggest business opportunities, driven by a growing population that needs to be fed. He notes that many global food and drink brands are built on agricultural products and urges African entrepreneurs to build their own brands around local produce.

Moving from selling raw crops to selling branded, processed products can raise incomes, create jobs and keep more value with farmers and local businesses.
cards.apply_it: Pick a crop or food your area is known for. What branded product could be made from it?

quiz.question: What opportunity does Masiyiwa see in African agriculture?
options: Building local brands around African produce
quiz.explanation: He urges entrepreneurs to brand and process local produce.
